Chapter overview

The Justice Party transformed early non-Brahmin mobilisation into provincial electoral government, communal representation, educational expansion, women’s political rights and a lasting social-justice framework before its transformation into Dravidar Kazhagam.

Origins & foundersManifesto & strategyMinistries & electionsRepresentation & reformDecline & transformation
Scope, Names and Historical Context

The Justice Party, officially the South Indian Liberal Federation, operated across the multilingual Madras Presidency and shaped provincial representation, administration and social policy from 1916 to 1944.

Official and Popular Names

The organisation’s official name was:

  • South Indian Liberal Federation
  • Commonly abbreviated as SILF

It became popularly known as the:

  • Justice Party
  • Neethi Katchi in Tamil usage

The popular name came from its English newspaper:

  • Justice

The organisation represented the first durable provincial political party organised primarily around non-Brahmin representation in the Madras Presidency.

Madras Presidency Context

The Justice Party operated throughout the Madras Presidency, which included substantial territories belonging to present-day:

  • Tamil Nadu
  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Kerala
  • Karnataka
  • Parts of Odisha

Its leaders therefore included Tamil-, Telugu-, Malayalam- and Kannada-speaking individuals.

The party should not be described as a Tamil Nadu-only organisation during its formative period.

Historical Period

The principal stages were:

  • 1916–1920 — Formation and political mobilisation
  • 1920–1926 — First period of Justice Party government
  • 1926–1930 — Period outside direct power
  • 1930–1937 — Return to government and gradual decline
  • 1937–1944 — Loss of electoral strength and ideological transformation
  • 1944 — Transformation into Dravidar Kazhagam
Importance

The Justice Party introduced organised demands for:

  • Non-Brahmin representation
  • Communal allocation in public employment
  • Wider educational access
  • Women’s political participation
  • Adi Dravida welfare
  • Regulation of religious endowments
  • Provincial social reform

Its methods were mainly constitutional and electoral rather than revolutionary.

Causes for the Rise of the Non-Brahmin Movement

The non-Brahmin movement arose from unequal access to English education, government employment, professional networks and representative institutions.

Unequal Access to English Education

English education expanded during the nineteenth century, but access was not equal across communities.

Early access to:

  • Schools
  • Colleges
  • Legal education
  • Professional qualifications
  • English-language employment

gave some groups a strong advantage in the colonial administrative system.

Non-Brahmin leaders argued that one socially advantaged group held a disproportionate number of positions in:

  • Government departments
  • Education
  • Law
  • Medicine
  • Journalism
  • Representative institutions
Government Employment

Modern government employment required:

  • English education
  • Examination success
  • Urban residence
  • Knowledge of official procedures
  • Access to professional networks

Many rural and socially disadvantaged communities lacked these opportunities.

The non-Brahmin movement therefore demanded:

  • Scholarships
  • Hostels
  • Wider school access
  • Communal representation
  • Fair recruitment
  • Promotion opportunities
Political Representation

Early nationalist organisations in Madras were dominated by educated urban elites.

Non-Brahmin leaders feared that immediate self-government without social safeguards might transfer power:

  • From British officials
  • To a narrow Indian social elite

They argued that political reform must be accompanied by:

  • Social reform
  • Educational equality
  • Community representation
Census and Community Identity

Colonial censuses classified people by:

  • Religion
  • Caste
  • Language
  • Occupation

These classifications encouraged communities to organise collectively and submit numerical claims for:

  • Employment
  • Education
  • Legislative seats
  • Public recognition
Influence of Earlier Movements

The Justice Party emerged after earlier organisations such as:

  • Madras Non-Brahmin Association
  • Madras United League
  • Madras Dravidian Association
  • Adi Dravida organisations
  • Community educational associations

It was therefore the political culmination of several earlier movements, not an organisation created suddenly in 1916.

Madras United League, Dravidian Association and Dravidian Home

The Madras United League, Dravidian Association and Dravidian Home converted employment and accommodation discrimination into organised social mobilisation.

Madras Non-Brahmin Association

The Madras Non-Brahmin Association was founded in:

  • 1909

Its founders included:

  • P. Subramaniam
  • M. Purushothama Naidu

Its main concerns were:

  • Education
  • Government employment
  • Non-Brahmin unity
  • Public representation

Its influence remained limited, but it provided an early organisational model.

Madras United League

The Madras United League was formed in:

  • 1912

It was supported mainly by non-Brahmin government employees who believed that they faced discrimination in:

  • Appointments
  • Promotion
  • Departmental advancement

A central organiser was:

  • Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar
Madras Dravidian Association

The Madras United League was subsequently renamed the:

  • Madras Dravidian Association

The term “Dravidian” was used to create a broad identity linking the non-Brahmin communities of South India.

Its activities included:

  • Adult-education classes
  • Public meetings
  • Support for graduates
  • Community organisation
  • Discussion of employment inequality
Dravidian Home

C. Natesa Mudaliar established the:

  • Dravidian Home
  • At Triplicane, Madras

The hostel provided accommodation for non-Brahmin students who faced discrimination in obtaining food and lodging in the city.

It offered:

  • Residence
  • Educational support
  • Social networks
  • Political awareness
Importance

These organisations created the social and organisational base from which the Justice Party emerged.

Essential association:

  • C. Natesa Mudaliar — Madras United League, Dravidian Association and Dravidian Home.
Formation and Founders of the Justice Party

The Justice Party was formed by provincial elites who believed constitutional reform required safeguards for non-Brahmin communities.

Formation

The South Indian Liberal Federation was established in:

  • November 1916
  • Madras

The formation brought together:

  • Landholders
  • Merchants
  • Doctors
  • Lawyers
  • Government employees
  • Community leaders
  • Urban professionals
Principal Founders

The three principal founders were:

  • P. Theagaraya Chetty
  • Dr. T. M. Nair
  • Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar
P. Theagaraya Chetty

Important associations:

  • Merchant and civic leader
  • Non-Brahmin political organisation
  • First prominent leader of the Justice Party
  • Madras Corporation
  • Educational and charitable activities

He declined the opportunity to become the first head of the provincial ministry after the 1920 election.

Dr. T. M. Nair

Important associations:

  • Medical doctor
  • Journalist
  • Political speaker
  • English-language propaganda
  • Justice newspaper
  • Advocacy before British political authorities

He died in 1919 before the party formed its first government.

Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar

Important associations:

  • Medical practitioner
  • Madras United League
  • Madras Dravidian Association
  • Dravidian Home
  • Organisational link between early non-Brahmin associations and the Justice Party
South Indian People’s Association

A closely related organisation called the:

  • South Indian People’s Association

was created to manage:

  • Newspapers
  • Printing
  • Propaganda
  • Public communication
Historical Importance

The founders did not hold identical social or political views.

What united them was the belief that constitutional reform must include safeguards for non-Brahmin communities.

Non-Brahmin Manifesto and Party Publications

The Non-Brahmin Manifesto and multilingual newspapers transformed social grievances into a province-wide political programme.

Non-Brahmin Manifesto

The Non-Brahmin Manifesto was issued in:

  • December 1916

It is also associated with the name:

  • Theagaraya Chetty’s Manifesto
Main Arguments

The manifesto argued that:

  • Government employment was distributed unequally.
  • Education was not equally accessible.
  • Representative institutions should reflect the Presidency’s diverse communities.
  • Immediate self-government without safeguards could produce elite domination.
  • Non-Brahmins required independent political organisation.
  • Political reform must be accompanied by social justice.

It did not call for the abolition of every caste distinction. Its immediate programme concentrated on representation and opportunity.

Justice

The English newspaper:

  • Justice

began publication in February 1917.

T. M. Nair was closely associated with its editorial direction.

The newspaper:

  • Explained party policy
  • Criticised Congress leadership
  • Defended communal representation
  • Reported non-Brahmin conferences
  • Opposed the Non-Cooperation Movement

Its popularity gave the organisation the name “Justice Party.”

Dravidan

The Tamil newspaper:

  • Dravidan

began publication in 1917.

It carried the movement’s arguments to Tamil readers and promoted:

  • Social reform
  • Non-Brahmin political consciousness
  • Educational advancement
  • Community representation
Andhra Prakasika

The movement was also associated with the Telugu newspaper:

  • Andhra Prakasika

This reflected the Presidency-wide character of the party.

Language Publications

The movement used newspapers in:

  • English
  • Tamil
  • Telugu
  • Malayalam

The press transformed a network of urban leaders into a province-wide political movement.

Objectives, Social Base and Political Strategy

The party combined social-justice objectives with constitutional cooperation, an elite social base and participation in colonial councils.

Main Objectives

The Justice Party sought:

  • Communal representation
  • Greater access to public employment
  • Educational opportunities
  • Scholarships and hostels
  • Legislative representation
  • Local-government participation
  • Social reform
  • Protection against elite monopoly
Constitutional Strategy

The party believed that reforms could be achieved through:

  • Elections
  • Legislative councils
  • Government Orders
  • Petitions
  • Negotiation with British authorities
  • Administrative measures

It rejected the Congress policy of boycotting the first elections under dyarchy.

Relationship with British Rule

The party cooperated with the colonial constitutional framework because it believed that:

  • The new councils provided access to power.
  • Representation could be secured through government action.
  • A Congress-led boycott would leave available seats uncontested.
  • British safeguards were temporarily necessary to prevent social monopoly.

This position allowed the Justice Party to implement reforms, but it also created a lasting criticism that the party was:

  • Loyalist
  • Pro-British
  • Insufficiently committed to independence
Social Base

The party’s leadership included many:

  • Landholders
  • Zamindars
  • Merchants
  • Professionals
  • Urban elites
  • Government employees

It claimed to represent all non-Brahmin communities, including oppressed groups.

However, its leadership did not always reflect:

  • Agricultural labourers
  • Industrial workers
  • Poor peasants
  • Adi Dravidas
  • Women
Political Tension

The party combined two different tendencies:

  • Social-justice demands
  • Elite constitutional politics

This combination produced both its major achievements and its later limitations.

Dyarchy, the 1920 Election and the First Justice Ministry

Dyarchy divided provincial subjects and enabled the Justice Party to form the first elected Madras ministry after the Congress boycott of 1920.

Government of India Act, 1919

The Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms introduced:

  • Dyarchy in the provinces
  • An enlarged legislative council
  • Limited provincial elections
Meaning of Dyarchy

Provincial subjects were divided into two categories.

Reserved Subjects

These remained under the Governor and his Executive Council.

They included major areas such as:

  • Finance
  • Police
  • Law and order
  • Revenue
Transferred Subjects

These were administered by Indian ministers responsible to the Legislative Council.

They included areas such as:

  • Education
  • Public health
  • Agriculture
  • Industries
  • Local self-government

Indian ministers therefore held office but did not control the entire provincial administration.

Election of 1920

The Indian National Congress boycotted the election as part of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

The Justice Party contested and won:

  • 63 of the 98 elected seats

The result gave it a clear majority.

P. Theagaraya Chetty’s Decision

Governor Lord Willingdon invited P. Theagaraya Chetty to form the ministry.

Theagaraya Chetty declined the position.

A. Subbarayalu Reddiar

A. Subbarayalu Reddiar became:

  • First Minister or Premier
  • Head of the first ministry formed under dyarchy
  • First head of a Justice Party government

His ministry began on:

  • 17 December 1920

Other important ministers included:

  • Raja of Panagal
  • K. V. Reddi Naidu

Subbarayalu Reddiar resigned in July 1921 because of ill health.

Historical Importance

The 1920 ministry was:

  • The first elected provincial ministry in Madras under dyarchy
  • The first government headed by the Justice Party
  • A major entry of organised non-Brahmin politics into administration

The official contemporary term was generally First Minister or Premier; “Chief Minister” is often used retrospectively.

Raja of Panagal and the Justice Ministry of 1921–1926

The Raja of Panagal’s long ministry became the party’s principal reforming phase within the restricted powers of dyarchy.

Raja of Panagal

Panaganti Ramarayaningar was popularly known as:

  • Raja of Panagal

He succeeded Subbarayalu Reddiar on:

  • 11 July 1921

He remained First Minister until:

  • 3 December 1926
Administrative Role

Under dyarchy, his government dealt mainly with transferred subjects such as:

  • Education
  • Local self-government
  • Public health
  • Agriculture
  • Industries

The limited powers of dyarchy restricted the ministry because important subjects remained under the Governor.

Major Associations

The Raja of Panagal is associated with:

  • Communal representation
  • Educational expansion
  • Adi Dravida welfare orders
  • Local-government reform
  • Religious-endowment regulation
  • Development of institutions
  • Expansion of the party organisation
Second Justice Ministry

After the 1923 election, the Justice Party remained in power and the Raja of Panagal continued as First Minister.

The party faced stronger opposition from:

  • Swarajists
  • Congress-aligned politicians
  • Dissident non-Brahmin leaders
  • Critics inside the Justice Party
T. Nagar

The development of the new residential locality later named:

  • Theagaraya Nagar
  • T. Nagar

occurred during the broader period of Justice administration and Madras city expansion.

It was named after:

  • P. Theagaraya Chetty
Importance

The Panagal ministry was the most important reforming phase of early Justice Party rule.

Many measures later identified with Tamil Nadu’s social-justice tradition were initiated or institutionalised during this period.

Elections of 1923 and 1926 and the Subbarayan Interlude

The elections of 1923 and 1926 exposed declining support, stronger Swarajist opposition and the distinction between Justice cabinets and the Subbarayan independent ministry.

Election of 1923

The Justice Party contested the second election under dyarchy.

It faced opposition from:

  • Swaraj Party
  • Independents
  • Internal dissidents

The Justice Party won the largest workable bloc and formed another ministry under:

  • Raja of Panagal

The party’s strength was lower than in 1920, showing that the political boycott advantage had begun to decline.

Reasons for Reduced Support

Important reasons included:

  • Growth of the Swaraj Party
  • Criticism of cooperation with British rule
  • Internal disputes
  • Regional disagreements
  • Exclusion of some Tamil leaders from high office
  • Dissatisfaction among oppressed communities
  • Criticism of elite leadership
Election of 1926

In the 1926 election:

  • The Justice Party failed to obtain a majority.
  • The Swaraj Party emerged as the strongest elected group.
  • The Swarajists refused to form a ministry under dyarchy.
P. Subbarayan Ministry

The Governor invited:

  • P. Subbarayan

to form an independent ministry.

The Subbarayan ministry lasted from:

  • 1926 to 1930

It was not initially a regular Justice Party ministry.

It survived through:

  • Governor’s support
  • Nominated members
  • Changing legislative alliances
  • Later cooperation from Justice Party groups
Important Measures During the Interlude

Some measures associated with the wider non-Brahmin social-justice programme developed during this period, including:

  • More effective communal allocation
  • Public Service Commission establishment
  • Higher-education expansion

These should not all be inaccurately labelled as measures passed by a Justice Party cabinet.

Essential Distinction
  • 1920 and 1923 — Justice Party ministries
  • 1926–1930 — P. Subbarayan’s independent ministry
  • 1930 — Justice Party returned to power.
Return to Power: Munuswamy Naidu and the Raja of Bobbili

The Justice Party returned in 1930 but economic depression, landlord factions and weak organisation reduced the effectiveness of its later ministries.

Election of 1930

The Congress again stayed away from the election because of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

The Justice Party returned to power.

B. Munuswamy Naidu

B. Munuswamy Naidu became First Minister in:

  • October 1930

His ministry faced:

  • Great Depression
  • Falling agricultural prices
  • Revenue difficulties
  • Floods
  • Landholder dissatisfaction
  • Internal party conflict
Zamindar–Non-Zamindar Division

Powerful landholders believed that the ministry had excluded their interests.

A faction developed around leaders including:

  • Raja of Bobbili
  • Kumara Raja of Venkatagiri
  • M. A. Muthiah Chettiar

Munuswamy Naidu resigned in:

  • November 1932
Raja of Bobbili

R. S. Ramakrishna Ranga Rao, the Raja of Bobbili, became First Minister on:

  • 5 November 1932

His period was affected by:

  • Great Depression
  • Agrarian distress
  • Factional conflict
  • Declining public support
  • Growing Congress nationalism
P. T. Rajan

P. T. Rajan briefly served as First Minister in:

  • 1936

The Raja of Bobbili later resumed office.

Final Interim Ministry

After the 1937 election, Congress initially delayed accepting office because of concerns regarding the Governor’s special powers.

K. V. Reddi Naidu headed an interim ministry for a brief period before:

  • Rajaji formed the Congress ministry
Significance

The later Justice ministries lacked the coherence of the Panagal period.

Elite factionalism and economic hardship weakened the party’s claim to represent the wider non-Brahmin population.

Communal Government Orders and Public-Service Representation

Communal Government Orders institutionalised group-based public-service representation and became a precursor of later reservation policy.

Meaning of Communal Representation

“Communal representation” referred to the allocation of public opportunities among identified communities.

The objective was to prevent one group from holding a disproportionate number of government posts.

First Communal Government Order

The Justice Party government issued:

  • G.O. No. 613
  • On 16 September 1921

It required departments to consider the representation of different communities in public appointments.

Second Government Order

A further order was issued in:

  • 1922

Department heads were directed to review whether communal representation was being followed.

Communities Considered

The system recognised categories including:

  • Non-Brahmin Hindus
  • Brahmins
  • Muslims
  • Indian Christians
  • Anglo-Indians
  • Depressed Classes or Adi Dravidas

The exact roster was developed and modified through later orders.

Implementation Difficulties

Early communal orders faced:

  • Administrative resistance
  • Legal challenges
  • Lack of reliable recruitment data
  • Departmental non-compliance
  • Disagreement over category proportions

The first orders established the principle, but implementation was gradual.

Staff Selection Board

A Staff Selection Board was created in:

  • 1924

It aimed to regularise recruitment and reduce uncontrolled departmental appointments.

Madras Public Service Commission

The Madras Public Service Commission was established in:

  • 1929

This occurred during the Subbarayan ministry, not under a regular Justice Party cabinet.

However, it developed from the wider demand for:

  • Fair recruitment
  • Open selection
  • Communal representation
  • Reduced departmental patronage
Historical Importance

The Communal G.O.s became a foundation for:

  • Reservation policy
  • Backward-class representation
  • Adi Dravida representation
  • Tamil Nadu’s later social-justice framework
Essential Caution

Do not confuse:

  • Communal G.O. of 1921 — Justice Party ministry
  • More detailed communal roster of the later 1920s — Subbarayan-period administration.
Education, Universities and Institutional Development

Justice-era educational policy expanded elementary education, disadvantaged-group access and university institutions across the Presidency.

Elementary Education

Justice Party ministries promoted the expansion of:

  • Elementary schools
  • Compulsory education
  • Girls’ education
  • Schools for disadvantaged communities
  • Grants to local bodies
  • Teacher recruitment

The Madras Elementary Education Act had been enacted in 1920, but Justice ministries participated in its implementation and expansion.

Compulsory Education

Local authorities were permitted or encouraged to introduce compulsory elementary education.

Parents could face penalties for unjustifiably withdrawing children from school in notified areas.

Education of Adi Dravida Students

Government measures included:

  • Mandatory admission to public schools
  • Threatened withdrawal of aid from schools refusing admission
  • Scholarships
  • Examination-fee concessions
  • Hostels
  • Medical and professional-education assistance
  • School construction in accessible locations
Madras University Act

The Madras University Act of:

  • 1923

reorganised the university and broadened its administrative structure.

Andhra University

The Andhra University legislation was passed in:

  • 1925

The university began functioning in:

  • 1926

Its creation responded to demands for higher education in the Telugu-speaking areas of the Presidency.

Annamalai University

The Annamalai University Act was enacted in:

  • 1928

The university opened in:

  • 1929

It was established with the support and endowment of:

  • S. R. M. Annamalai Chettiar

It encouraged higher education and research in the Tamil districts.

Midday Meal: Historical Caution

A school feeding initiative began in the Madras Corporation during:

  • 1920
  • At a school in the Thousand Lights area

P. Theagaraya Chetty was closely connected with Madras municipal administration.

The programme was a municipal initiative, not a province-wide Justice Party midday-meal law.

Importance

The party regarded education as the main route to:

  • Public employment
  • Social mobility
  • Political representation
  • Reduction of inherited inequality.
Women’s Franchise and Legislative Social Reform

The Justice period opened qualified franchise and legislative office to women while creating space for Muthulakshmi Reddy’s reform agenda.

Women’s Voting Rights

The first Justice ministry supported the removal of sex-based restrictions on political participation.

In:

  • 1921

the Madras Legislative Council adopted a measure enabling qualified women to obtain voting rights.

The franchise was not universal.

It depended on qualifications such as:

  • Property
  • Tax payment
  • Education
  • Marital status under existing electoral rules

Nevertheless, Madras became one of the earliest provinces to enfranchise women.

Eligibility for Legislative Membership

The Justice administration also supported gender-neutral eligibility for legislative participation.

This opened the path for women to become:

  • Voters
  • Candidates
  • Legislators
Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy

Muthulakshmi Reddy was nominated to the Madras Legislative Council in:

  • 1926

She became the first woman legislator in British India.

She later became:

  • Deputy President of the Council
Main Reform Concerns

Muthulakshmi Reddy worked for:

  • Women’s education
  • Public health
  • Child welfare
  • Marriage reform
  • Prevention of Devadasi dedication
  • Protection of vulnerable girls
  • Women’s political rights
Devadasi Reform: Historical Caution

Muthulakshmi Reddy introduced measures against Devadasi dedication during the late 1920s.

However:

  • The debate produced support and opposition within different political groups.
  • The final Madras Devadasis Prevention of Dedication Act was passed only in 1947.
  • It is inaccurate to claim that the Justice Party completed abolition through a law in the 1920s.
Importance

The Justice Party period created the institutional space through which women moved from reform associations into:

  • Voting
  • Legislative membership
  • Public administration
  • Law-making.
Adi Dravida Welfare, Representation and Its Limitations

Justice governments issued major Adi Dravida welfare measures, but elite non-Brahmin politics did not eliminate caste inequality within non-Brahmin society.

Official Use of “Adi Dravida”

M. C. Rajah introduced a resolution seeking the replacement of derogatory official names.

The government issued an order in:

  • March 1922

directing the use of:

  • Adi Dravida

in official documents.

The term expressed:

  • Dignity
  • Original inhabitant identity
  • Rejection of insulting caste terminology
Educational Measures

Justice-era orders directed that:

  • Adi Dravida children must be admitted to public schools.
  • Aided schools refusing admission could lose financial support.
  • Children should not be segregated into separate classrooms.
  • Schools should be built in locations accessible to oppressed communities.
  • Scholarships and stipends should be provided.
  • Examination fees should be waived in specified cases.
  • Hostels should be established.
Land and Housing

Measures included:

  • House-site pattas
  • Panchami land distribution
  • Residential assistance
  • Support for hostels and schools
Public-Space Access

Orders were issued against preventing Adi Dravidas from using:

  • Public roads
  • Common wells
  • Government offices
  • Public lodges
  • Other civic spaces
Government Employment

Communal representation created limited opportunities in:

  • Police service
  • Provincial departments
  • Local bodies
  • Professional education
Political Representation

Important Adi Dravida leaders during the period included:

  • M. C. Rajah
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan
  • L. C. Gurusami
  • Swami Sahajananda
  • Other local organisers
Limitations and Conflicts

The Justice Party claimed to represent all non-Brahmins, but its relationship with Adi Dravida organisations was not always harmonious.

Major limitations included:

  • Dominance of affluent non-Brahmin elites
  • Inadequate Adi Dravida leadership within the party
  • Conflicts between intermediate castes and oppressed communities
  • Labour disputes
  • Unequal implementation of welfare orders
  • Different demands for separate political safeguards

The Pulianthope labour conflict of 1921 exposed tensions between:

  • Labour politics
  • Caste identities
  • Justice Party leadership
  • Adi Dravida mobilisation
Balanced Assessment

Justice governments issued significant welfare and access orders.

However, non-Brahmin politics and Adi Dravida politics were not identical, and the party did not eliminate caste oppression within non-Brahmin society.

Religious Endowments, Local Government and Economic Measures

Religious-endowment regulation, local administration and state aid to industry reveal the party’s wider administrative programme and the limitations of dyarchy.

Hindu Religious Endowments

Justice Party leaders argued that temples receiving public donations and controlling extensive property required:

  • Financial accountability
  • Public supervision
  • Protection from hereditary mismanagement

Religious-endowment legislation was introduced during the early Justice ministries.

The Madras Hindu Religious Endowments legislation was passed in:

  • 1925

It established a statutory framework for supervising many Hindu religious institutions.

Objectives

The legislation aimed to regulate:

  • Temple income
  • Property
  • Endowments
  • Trustee administration
  • Financial records
  • Misuse of funds

It established the basis for the later Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments system.

Historical Debate

Supporters viewed regulation as:

  • Public accountability
  • Protection of temple property
  • Reduction of hereditary monopoly

Critics viewed it as:

  • Government interference in religion
  • Reduction of institutional autonomy

Detailed rationalist criticism of temple worship belongs to Chapters 23, 24 and 28.

Local Self-Government

Justice ministries worked through:

  • Municipalities
  • District boards
  • Local boards
  • Public-health bodies

Areas of activity included:

  • Roads
  • Sanitation
  • Drinking water
  • Schools
  • Hospitals
  • Housing
  • Urban planning
Town Planning

Madras city expanded through:

  • Planned residential areas
  • Road development
  • Municipal extension
  • Drainage and sanitation projects

The development of Theagaraya Nagar is associated with this phase.

State Aid to Industries

The State Aid to Industries Act of:

  • 1922

allowed government assistance and loans for industrial development.

Agricultural and Tenancy Measures

Justice administrations addressed:

  • Agricultural improvement
  • Irrigation demands within the limits of dyarchy
  • Cooperative credit
  • Tenant protection
  • Rural development

The Malabar Tenancy Act of 1931 gave certain protections to tenants in the Malabar region.

Limitation of Dyarchy

Justice ministers controlled transferred departments but lacked full authority over:

  • Finance
  • Police
  • Major revenue policy
  • Law and order

Their administrative record must therefore be assessed within the restricted constitutional framework.

Decline, Periyar’s Leadership and Transformation into Dravidar Kazhagam

Electoral decline, Periyar’s leadership and the 1944 Salem resolutions transformed an electoral provincial party into the non-electoral Dravidar Kazhagam.

Relationship with the Congress

The Justice Party opposed the Congress on several questions.

Justice Party Position
  • Contested elections under dyarchy
  • Cooperated constitutionally with British rule
  • Prioritised communal representation
  • Feared elite domination under immediate self-rule
Congress Position
  • Led the national freedom struggle
  • Boycotted the 1920 elections
  • Used Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience
  • Criticised Justice collaboration with colonial rule

The relationship was not simply “nationalist versus social reform.”

Both organisations contained social divisions and changed over time.

Reasons for Decline
Pro-British Image

The party’s cooperation with colonial government became unpopular as nationalism expanded.

Elite Leadership

Many leaders were:

  • Zamindars
  • Wealthy merchants
  • Professionals
  • Urban elites

The organisation often lacked sustained grassroots mobilisation.

Internal Factionalism

Major divisions included:

  • Tamil versus Telugu leadership disputes
  • Zamindar versus non-zamindar factions
  • Ministerial rivalries
  • Personal conflicts
  • Disputes over party control
Weak Labour and Peasant Base

The party did not consistently organise:

  • Industrial workers
  • Poor tenants
  • Agricultural labourers
  • Landless communities
Adi Dravida Alienation

Some Adi Dravida leaders believed that the party’s broad non-Brahmin category concealed continuing caste inequality.

Growth of Congress

The Congress expanded through:

  • Civil Disobedience
  • Khadi
  • Rural organisation
  • Labour participation
  • Nationalist sentiment
Election of 1937

The Government of India Act of 1935 created a larger provincial legislature and expanded the electorate.

In the 1937 election:

  • The Congress achieved a major victory.
  • The Justice Party suffered a severe defeat.
  • Rajaji later formed the Congress ministry.

The Justice Party never recovered its former electoral strength.

Periyar’s Leadership

After the defeat, E. V. Ramasamy became increasingly influential within the party.

He was elected party president in:

  • 1938

He brought the party closer to:

  • Rationalism
  • Self-Respect principles
  • Caste abolition
  • Women’s equality
  • Anti-Hindi mobilisation
  • Criticism of religious authority

His complete political and social contribution belongs to Chapter 28.

Salem Conference of 1944

At the Salem conference held on:

  • 27 August 1944

the organisation adopted major changes.

Members were asked to:

  • Renounce British titles
  • Give up nominated government posts
  • Remove caste suffixes
  • Withdraw from electoral politics
  • Commit to social transformation

The Justice Party was transformed into:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • DK

C. N. Annadurai played an important role in presenting and supporting the resolutions.

Essential Distinction

Periyar:

  • Did not found the Justice Party.
  • Became its leader more than twenty years after its formation.
  • Transformed it into Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.

The detailed history of Dravidar Kazhagam belongs to Chapters 25, 27 and 28.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, founders, ministries, Government Orders, institutions and the distinctions most frequently tested in TNPSC examinations.

High-Yield Distinctions
South Indian Liberal Federation versus Justice Party

They refer to the same principal organisation.

  • Official name — South Indian Liberal Federation
  • Popular name — Justice Party
Justice Party versus Justice Newspaper

Justice Party

  • Political organisation
  • Founded in 1916

Justice

  • English newspaper
  • Began in 1917
  • Gave the party its popular name
Madras United League versus Justice Party

Madras United League

  • 1912
  • Government employees and social organisation
  • Precursor

Justice Party

  • 1916
  • Political party
  • Contested elections and formed ministries
Non-Brahmin Manifesto versus Communal G.O.

Non-Brahmin Manifesto

  • 1916
  • Political statement
  • Explained grievances and demands

Communal G.O.

  • 1921 onward
  • Administrative order
  • Applied representation principles to public employment
Communal Representation versus Reservation

Communal representation

  • Historical Presidency terminology
  • Distribution among listed communities

Reservation

  • Later constitutional and administrative terminology
  • Corrective representation for disadvantaged groups
Subbarayalu Reddiar versus Raja of Panagal

Subbarayalu Reddiar

  • First Justice Party head of government
  • December 1920–July 1921

Raja of Panagal

  • Longest early Justice ministry
  • July 1921–December 1926
  • Major social-justice measures
1926 Ministry versus 1930 Ministry

1926

  • Justice Party lost majority
  • P. Subbarayan formed independent ministry

1930

  • Justice Party returned
  • B. Munuswamy Naidu became First Minister
Justice Party versus Congress

Justice Party

  • Electoral participation under dyarchy
  • Communal representation
  • Constitutional cooperation
  • Non-Brahmin social justice

Congress

  • National independence
  • Mass movements
  • Boycott and Civil Disobedience
  • Increasing rural mobilisation
Justice Party versus Self-Respect Movement

Justice Party

  • Electoral party
  • Government employment and representation
  • Worked within colonial councils

Self-Respect Movement

  • Social movement
  • Caste abolition
  • Rationalism
  • Marriage and gender reform
Justice Party versus Dravidar Kazhagam

Justice Party

  • Formed in 1916
  • Contested elections
  • Formed provincial governments

Dravidar Kazhagam

  • Formed through transformation in 1944
  • Led by Periyar
  • Withdrew from electoral politics
  • Concentrated on social transformation
Periyar versus Justice Party Founders

Founders

  • Theagaraya Chetty
  • T. M. Nair
  • C. Natesa Mudaliar

Periyar

  • Did not found the party
  • Became president in 1938
  • Transformed it into DK in 1944
Non-Brahmin versus Adi Dravida Politics

Non-Brahmin politics

  • Broad coalition outside Brahmin communities
  • Representation and public employment

Adi Dravida politics

  • Focused on communities subjected to untouchability
  • Civil rights, land, education and separate safeguards

The two were connected but not identical.

Exam Traps
  • The official name was South Indian Liberal Federation.
  • Justice Party was its popular name.
  • The party was founded in 1916; the Justice newspaper began in 1917.
  • Periyar was not a founder.
  • T. M. Nair died before the party formed its first government.
  • P. Theagaraya Chetty declined the first ministership.
  • A. Subbarayalu Reddiar headed the first Justice ministry.
  • Raja of Panagal succeeded Subbarayalu Reddiar.
  • Justice Party won 63 of 98 elected seats in 1920.
  • The first Communal G.O. was issued in 1921.
  • Adi Dravida became an official administrative term in 1922.
  • The Staff Selection Board was created in 1924.
  • The Public Service Commission was created in 1929 during the Subbarayan period.
  • P. Subbarayan’s ministry was not initially a regular Justice Party ministry.
  • The Justice Party returned to power in 1930.
  • Muthulakshmi Reddy was the first woman legislator in British India.
  • The final Devadasi abolition law belongs to 1947, not the early Justice ministries.
  • Hindu religious-endowment regulation developed during Justice Party rule.
  • Justice Party suffered a major defeat in 1937.
  • Periyar became party president after the 1937 defeat.
  • Justice Party became Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.
  • The detailed Self-Respect Movement belongs to Chapter 24.
  • The detailed Dravidian Movement belongs to Chapter 25.
  • Periyar’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 28.
  • Anna’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 29.
